d.g: The logic function exclusive OR (as opposed to inclusive OR), whose output is true only when exactly one of its inputs is true.
The connective "exclusive or". One way to state its meaning in plain English is "if either A or B, but not if both."
d.x: The XOR of (0,0) is 0; (0,1) is 1; (1,0) is 1; and (1,1) is 0.

d.g: A wind over Lake Atitlan in Guatemala.

Xocomil.e: Borrowed from Spanish Xocomil, from Kaqchikel Xokomil, from xokom (“left; south”).

d.g: A hydrous silicate of calcium, occurring in massive form of a white or bluish‐gray colour.
A logic gate performing a Boolean logic XOR operation.
d.x: The output of the XOR gate is logic 1 or high, when its inputs are dissimilar.

d.g: A spicy sauce from Hong Kong, made from roughly chopped dried seafood, chili peppers, onions, and garlic.

XO sauce.e: From the name of fine XO (extra-old) cognac, which (though not an ingredient of the sauce) denotes high quality, prestige, and luxury in Hong Kong.

d.g: A former employee of the Google corporation.
d.x: Older Googlers with families tend to like it less, because "everybody, even young mums, works seven days a week." Another Xoogler, who held a senior position, says that by trying to create a "Utopia" of untrammelled creativity, Google ended up with "dystopia".

d.g: A municipality of Guerrero, Mexico. Capital: Xochistlahuaca.

Xochistlahuaca.e: Borrowed from Spanish Xochistlahuaca, from a Nahuan language; equivalent to Classical Nahuatl xōchitl (“flower”) + ixtlāhuacān (“plain”). The Nahuan word is a calque from Amuzgo; compare San Pedro Amuzgos Amuzgo Suntjaaꞌ (“flower plain”).

d.g: A town in Alcozauca de Guerrero, Guerrero, Mexico.

Xochapa.e: Borrowed from Spanish Xochapa, from a Nahuan language (equivalent to Classical Nahuatl xōchitl (“flower”) + āpan (“river”)), calqued from a Mixtec language, e.g. Alcozauca Mixtec I̱ta Ita (literally “flower river”).
